actions.result: Bilateral tonsillar enlargement with white-gray exudate, erythematous posterior pharynx, no uvular deviation, no asymmetric bulging

actions.result: Patient reports tender, mobile, enlarged lymph nodes in anterior and posterior cervical chains bilaterally, largest about 2 cm, also tender nodes behind the ears (posterior auricular); no fixed or rock-hard nodes

actions.result: Patient reports mild fullness and tenderness to palpation in the left upper quadrant beneath the ribs, no rebound, no guarding; cannot reliably assess organ edge via self-exam

actions.name: Camera inspection of skin for rash
actions.result: No rash visible on face, trunk, or arms shown on camera

actions.name: Visual assessment of work of breathing and voice
actions.result: Speaking in full sentences, no stridor, no drooling, voice slightly muffled but understandable, no visible respiratory distress

actions.name: Review rapid strep (rapid antigen detection) test result from student health visit yesterday
actions.result: Rapid strep antigen test: Negative (performed at student health center yesterday)

actions.name: Order/review complete blood count with differential
actions.result: WBC 12.8 x10^3/uL (H), with 68% lymphocytes (H) including 22% atypical lymphocytes (H); Hemoglobin 14.2 g/dL, Platelets 210 x10^3/uL

actions.name: Order/review liver function tests (ALT, AST, bilirubin)
actions.result: ALT 86 U/L (H), AST 72 U/L (H), Total bilirubin 0.9 mg/dL (normal)

actions.name: Order/review throat culture (bacterial)
actions.result: Throat culture pending at time of visit; no growth of Group A Streptococcus reported after 48 hours (reported in follow-up note)

actions.name: Review student health center visit note from yesterday
actions.result: Visit note: sore throat x5 days, fever, fatigue; rapid strep negative; advised to rest and follow up if worsening; no antibiotics given

actions.name: Review current medication list
actions.result: No prescription medications; occasional ibuprofen 400 mg PRN for pain/fever

actions.name: Order abdominal ultrasound to assess spleen size
actions.result: Not performed at this visit; would require in-person imaging order and is not indicated urgently given reassuring exam and absence of trauma or severe pain

artifacts.body:
CC: Sore throat, fever x5 days.
HPI: 20 yo male with 5 days sore throat, fever to 101F, fatigue, neck swelling. Roommate had 'strep throat' approximately 4 weeks ago.
Exam: Tonsillar erythema and exudate, tender bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy. No respiratory distress.
Rapid strep antigen test: Negative.
Throat culture sent, pending.
Plan: Supportive care - fluids, rest, acetaminophen/ibuprofen for fever and pain. Return precautions given for worsening symptoms, difficulty breathing/swallowing, or inability to tolerate fluids. Follow up in 2-3 days or sooner if worse.

[Addendum, +48h]: Throat culture: No growth of Group A Streptococcus.

mismatches.patientClaim: Patient reports the rapid strep test done at student health yesterday was negative, and believes this means he does not have strep and is looking for another explanation
mismatches.recordEvidence: Student health note confirms rapid strep negative, but also shows throat culture was sent and addendum shows it later confirmed negative too (no growth of Group A Streptococcus) - consistent with patient's report, but the mismatch for teaching is that despite negative strep testing, the roommate's antibiotic treatment makes the patient expect he too needs antibiotics (see f31), when the actual diagnosis is viral (mono) and antibiotics are not indicated and amoxicillin specifically should be avoided
mismatches.teachingPoint: A negative strep test with compatible symptoms (exudative pharyngitis, tender lymphadenopathy, profound fatigue, splenic tenderness) in a young adult should prompt testing for mononucleosis rather than empiric antibiotics; amoxicillin/ampicillin can cause a non-allergic rash in mono and should be avoided.

objectives.text: Elicit a focused history that distinguishes infectious mononucleosis from streptococcal pharyngitis, including exposure history, fever pattern, lymphadenopathy distribution, and fatigue severity.
Recognize posterior cervical and posterior auricular lymphadenopathy and splenic tenderness as findings supportive of mononucleosis over bacterial pharyngitis.
Order and correctly interpret confirmatory testing (heterophile antibody, CBC with differential, liver enzymes) to support the diagnosis of infectious mononucleosis.
Counsel the patient on activity restriction, specifically avoiding contact sports such as rugby for 3-4 weeks due to splenic rupture risk, balancing the patient's goals with safety.
Explain why antibiotics, especially amoxicillin/ampicillin, are not indicated and may cause a rash, addressing the patient's expectation based on his roommate's treatment.
Identify red-flag symptoms requiring urgent escalation, including airway compromise and severe abdominal pain suggestive of splenic rupture.

scenario.studentBrief: You are seeing Arjun Mehta, a 20-year-old college student, via telehealth video visit for 6 days of sore throat, fever, and fatigue. He was seen at student health yesterday where a rapid strep test was negative. Take a focused history, perform feasible remote examination maneuvers, order appropriate testing, and develop a management plan.
scenario.chiefComplaint: Sore throat, fever, swollen neck glands, and fatigue for 6 days
scenario.openingLine: Hi, thanks for seeing me. I've had this awful sore throat and fever for about six days now, and I'm just exhausted all the time. My neck glands feel swollen too.
tasks: Obtain a focused history of present illness including exposure history and associated symptoms
Guide the patient through feasible remote examination maneuvers (throat inspection, lymph node and abdominal self-palpation)
Order and interpret appropriate laboratory testing
Formulate a working diagnosis and differential, and counsel the patient on management
Address the patient's concerns and agree on a plan with safety-netting

differential: Streptococcal pharyngitis (less likely given negative rapid antigen and culture)
Acute HIV infection (consider if risk factors present)
keyFindings: 6 days of sore throat, fever to 38.6°C, profound fatigue
Negative rapid strep antigen test and negative throat culture
Bilateral tender cervical and posterior auricular lymphadenopathy
Exudative tonsillar pharyngitis on camera exam
Left upper quadrant fullness/tenderness suggestive of splenomegaly
Atypical lymphocytosis on CBC with mild transaminitis
plan: Confirm diagnosis with heterophile antibody test and CBC with differential (completed, both support mononucleosis)
Check liver enzymes given hepatic involvement is common in mono (completed, mildly elevated)
Supportive care: rest, hydration, acetaminophen or ibuprofen for fever/pain, avoid amoxicillin/ampicillin given risk of non-allergic rash in mono

Advise strict avoidance of contact sports and rugby for at least 3-4 weeks due to risk of splenic rupture; reassess before clearing return to play, possibly with splenic size assessment if symptoms persist
Educate on warning signs requiring urgent/emergency care: difficulty breathing or swallowing, severe or worsening left upper quadrant or abdominal pain, lightheadedness, or signs of bleeding
Arrange follow-up in 1-2 weeks to reassess symptoms, fatigue, and readiness to resume activity; consider repeat exam before any contact sport clearance
No antibiotics indicated as this is a viral illness
redFlags: Difficulty breathing, stridor, or drooling suggesting airway compromise from tonsillar swelling
Severe or worsening left upper quadrant abdominal pain or lightheadedness suggesting splenic rupture - requires emergency evaluation
Inability to tolerate oral fluids leading to dehydration
Persistent high fever beyond 10-14 days or signs of secondary bacterial infection
educationPoints: Mononucleosis is caused by Epstein-Barr virus and commonly presents with the triad of fever, pharyngitis, and lymphadenopathy, often with marked fatigue
A negative rapid strep test and throat culture, combined with posterior cervical/auricular adenopathy and profound fatigue, should prompt testing for mono rather than empiric antibiotics
Amoxicillin and ampicillin should be avoided in mononucleosis due to the well-described non-allergic morbilliform rash that can occur
Contact and collision sports should be avoided for at least 3-4 weeks from symptom onset due to the risk of splenic rupture, even without a palpable spleen on exam
Mild transaminitis and atypical lymphocytosis are common and expected laboratory findings in acute mono and do not require specific treatment
Fatigue in mono can persist for weeks and patients should be counseled about gradual return to activity

profile.summary: A healthy 20-year-old college student presents via telehealth with 6 days of sore throat, fever, fatigue, and cervical lymphadenopathy following a negative rapid strep test, teaching learners to recognize infectious mononucleosis through history, remote exam maneuvers, and confirmatory labs. The case emphasizes avoiding amoxicillin, counseling on contact sport restriction for splenic rupture risk, and addressing a patient's expectation of needing antibiotics.
